name: Cork & Cobh
tagline: Ireland's proudly independent second city, and the colourful harbour town where millions of emigrants took their last look at home.
highlight: Standing at the rail of Cobh's harbourfront, looking out at the exact spot where the Titanic made her final stop before crossing the Atlantic.
shortDescription: Ireland's food-loving second city and the historic harbour town of Cobh, the Titanic's last port of call and the departure point for millions of Irish emigrants.
metaDescription: A Cork and Cobh travel guide: the English Market, Blarney Castle, the Titanic Experience, food and how to plan a visit to Ireland's southwest coast.
knownFor: The English Market, Blarney Castle, Titanic history
goodFor: Food, history, an easy coastal day trip

intro: Cork is genuinely Ireland's proudly independent second city, self-styled as the 'real capital' and built around a genuinely excellent food scene centred on the historic English Market.

A short train ride away sits Cobh, a genuinely colourful harbour town stacked up a steep hillside beneath St Colman's Cathedral, forever tied to the Titanic as her final port of call and to the millions of Irish emigrants who left from here for America.
Most visitors genuinely combine the two as an easy day trip or overnight, pairing Cork's food and history with Cobh's more sobering, genuinely moving maritime story.

whyVisit.intro: Cork and Cobh's case rests on genuinely excellent food and a maritime history found nowhere else in Ireland.

points.title: The English Market is genuinely one of Europe's great food markets
points.text: A covered Victorian market hall of local producers, still the beating heart of Cork's food culture.

points.title: Cobh's Titanic connection is genuinely direct, not just thematic
points.text: The actual last port of call before the ship's fatal Atlantic crossing in 1912.

points.title: Blarney Castle is genuinely just outside the city
points.text: Home to the famous Blarney Stone, said to grant the gift of eloquence to those who kiss it.

points.title: Cork's food scene is genuinely a step ahead of its size
points.text: A proudly independent culinary identity, distinct from Dublin's, built around local produce.

points.title: Cobh's hillside houses are genuinely photogenic
points.text: Brightly painted terraces stacked beneath the cathedral, overlooking one of the world's largest natural harbours.

attractionsIntro: Cork and Cobh's essential sights combine a genuinely excellent food city with a direct link to maritime history.

attractions.name: The English Market

image.alt: The covered Victorian English Market in Cork

attractions.text: Genuinely one of Europe's oldest and best covered markets, trading continuously since 1788, and still Cork's food culture at its core.
attractions.tip: Genuinely arrive hungry — the market's food stalls make for an excellent, informal lunch.

attractions.name: Blarney Castle & the Blarney Stone

image.alt: Blarney Castle near Cork, home of the Blarney Stone

attractions.text: A genuinely atmospheric 15th-century castle just outside the city, famous for the stone said to grant the gift of eloquence to those who kiss it.
attractions.tip: Genuinely visit early in the day to avoid the longest queues for the stone itself.

attractions.name: St Fin Barre's Cathedral

image.alt: The Gothic Revival spires of St Fin Barre's Cathedral in Cork

attractions.text: A genuinely striking Gothic Revival cathedral with three spires, built on a site with religious use stretching back to the 7th century.
attractions.tip: The genuinely golden angel atop the east end is said to sound its trumpet on Judgment Day, according to local legend.

attractions.name: Cork City Gaol

image.alt: The Victorian former prison building of Cork City Gaol

attractions.text: A genuinely striking Victorian former prison, now a museum with restored cells telling the stories of its former inmates.
attractions.tip: The genuinely audio guide included with entry is unusually well done, worth the extra time.

attractions.name: Titanic Experience Cobh

image.alt: The Titanic Experience museum in Cobh

attractions.text: Genuinely housed in the original White Star Line ticket office, from where the last passengers boarded a tender out to the Titanic in 1912.
attractions.tip: Genuinely book ahead in summer — the guided tour format means timed entry can sell out.

attractions.name: St Colman's Cathedral, Cobh

image.alt: St Colman's Cathedral overlooking the town of Cobh

attractions.text: A genuinely striking neo-Gothic cathedral towering over Cobh's hillside, its 49-bell carillon among the largest in Europe.
attractions.tip: Genuinely check for carillon recital times — the bells are audible across the whole town.

attractions.name: Cobh's harbourfront

image.alt: The colourful harbourfront houses of Cobh

attractions.text: Genuinely one of Ireland's most photogenic waterfronts, brightly painted terraced houses stacked up the hillside above one of the world's largest natural harbours.
attractions.tip: Genuinely the best photo angle is from the water itself, or the hillside streets just above the front.

thingsToDoIntro: Cork and Cobh genuinely reward pairing a food-focused city day with a more reflective afternoon by the harbour.

thingsToDo.title: Browse the English Market

image.alt: Stalls inside Cork's English Market

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely essential Cork morning, wandering stalls of local cheese, fish, meat and baked goods under Victorian ironwork.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely the market gets busiest around lunchtime — an earlier visit is calmer.

thingsToDo.title: Kiss the Blarney Stone

image.alt: Visitors climbing Blarney Castle to kiss the Blarney Stone

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely iconic, slightly odd Irish tradition, leaning backward over the castle battlements to kiss the stone below.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely wear comfortable shoes — the spiral staircase to the top is narrow and steep.

thingsToDo.title: Wander Blarney Castle's gardens

image.alt: The grounds and gardens surrounding Blarney Castle

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely underrated part of the visit, extensive gardens, a rock close and woodland walks beyond the castle itself.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely budget an extra hour beyond the castle for the gardens — many visitors skip them.

thingsToDo.title: Learn Cork's history at the City Gaol

image.alt: The restored cell blocks of Cork City Gaol

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely engaging way to spend a couple of hours, restored cells and exhibits telling real stories from the prison's history.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely combine with the on-site Radio Museum, an unexpected bonus included with entry.

thingsToDo.title: Trace Titanic history in Cobh

image.file: File:The Titanic Experience, Casement Square, Cobh - geograph.org.uk - 5851985.jpg
image.alt: The Titanic Experience building in Cobh's town square

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely moving way to spend an hour, following the last passengers' footsteps from ticket office to tender boat.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely combine with the nearby Cobh Heritage Centre for the broader emigration story.

thingsToDo.title: Walk Cobh's colourful harbourfront

image.alt: A walk along Cobh's colourful harbourfront

thingsToDo.text: A genuinely easy, scenic stroll along the water, with views out to one of the world's largest natural harbours.
thingsToDo.tip: Genuinely climb the hillside streets above the front for the classic postcard view back down.

foods.text: Genuinely the best way to taste Cork, sampling artisan cheese, fresh fish and baked goods straight from the market's stalls.

foods.text: A genuinely Cork specialty, the city long credited with perfecting the recipe for both styles of pudding.
foods.whereToTry: Butchers and breakfast menus throughout the city.

foods.text: A genuinely reliable choice by the harbour in Cobh, made with the day's fresh catch.

foods.text: Genuinely a point of local pride — Cork has its own stout tradition distinct from Dublin's, alongside the national favourite.

foods.name: Irish stew

foods.text: A genuinely warming classic found on menus throughout the city and in Cobh's harbourside pubs.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional restaurants throughout Cork and Cobh.

bestTime.headline: May to September for the best weather, though both work year-round
bestTime.summary: Cork and Cobh are genuinely enjoyable in any season, given their indoor markets and museums, though outdoor sightseeing is best in the warmer months.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Cork and Cobh visit noticeably smoother.
tips: Visit Blarney Castle genuinely early in the day to avoid the longest queues.
Book Titanic Experience tickets genuinely ahead in summer, given the timed guided tour format.
Arrive at the English Market genuinely hungry — it's one of the best lunch options in the city.
Take the genuinely short train to Cobh rather than driving — parking there is limited.
Wear genuinely comfortable shoes for Cobh's steep hillside streets.
Check genuinely carillon recital times at St Colman's Cathedral if visiting on a whim.

faq.q: How many days do you need for Cork and Cobh?
faq.a: Two days genuinely covers both comfortably, though Cobh alone is an easy half-day or full-day trip from Cork.

faq.q: Can you visit Cobh as a day trip from Cork?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely easily — a direct local train takes about 25 minutes each way, running frequently.
Yes, genuinely — beyond the famous stone, the castle grounds and gardens are worth a couple of hours on their own.
Genuinely its independent food scene centred on the English Market, and its proud identity as Ireland's 'real capital.'

faq.q: Why is Cobh significant to Titanic history?
faq.a: Genuinely the ship's last port of call before crossing the Atlantic in 1912, and from where its final passengers boarded by tender.

faq.q: Is Cork worth visiting if you're short on time in Ireland?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely — even a single day covers the English Market and city centre well, with Cobh or Blarney as an easy addition.
